newsitem.title: FRANCE: France seen sticking to EMU even if left wins.
newsitem.headline: France seen sticking to EMU even if left wins.

text.p: France is expected to stick to its commitment to launch a single European currency in 1999 even if a left-wing lead in a first-round parliamentary election vote translates into victory in next Sundays second-round runoff.

But economists said financial markets were in for a bumpy ride in the next few days simply because any change in the European political landscape would unnerve those who still feared an unravelling of plans for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Polling institute projections by 2100 GMT showed the opposition Socialist and Communist parties narrowly leading the ruling centre-right UDF/RPR coalition in terms of votes and number of confirmed seats in the National Assembly.

The early results sparked a flight into marks from other European currencies in light overnight trading and economists predicted a drop in the franc, stocks and bonds on Monday on fears a Socialist government might be less committed to EMU.

But they said they believed that on balance a Socialist government would do what it needed to do -- including making power-sharing with conservative President Jacques Chirac workable -- to get the euro currency launched on time.
"They don't have a choice," Daiwa Research Institute economist Bernard Godement said.
Of all the countries involved in the EMU plans, France may have the most to lose if the project is abandoned.

It put up with years of high interest rates to keep a link between the franc and the German mark, seen here as the linchpin of a single currency, and is only now beginning to reap the benefits of a lower cost of credit.
Giving up would be to admit that the years of sacrifice, including round after round of austerity, had been in vain.
"I am sure the Socialists would remain committed to monetary union," UBS economist Darren Williams said.

Any confirmation of a Socialist victory next Sunday would nonetheless come at a delicate time for EMU, a time when Germany has unnerved markets and domestic opinion alike with plans to revalue its gold reserves to bolster its public finances.
So any fears a new Socialist government would be less likely to implement austerity to prepare France for EMU would send jitters throughout European markets.
"The franc is weakening. It could be negative for the lira and the peseta as well," ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard said.
"I think that this week is going to be very turbulent," Nomura economist Sonja Gibbs said.

"Other European markets will suffer as people worry about EMU uncertainties, True, the Socialists have been making all the right sounds for EMU, saying 'yes' we are for EMU, but the conditions they are attaching to France's participation in EMU are really onerous," she added.

The Socialists have set four conditions for backing EMU -- a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht treaty, a European "economic government", a euro not overvalued against the dollar and a new pact for Europe to work together for growth.

These conditions are not that different from those of the centre-right. Both mainstream parties share a common French vision of Europe, where strong political input would balance the power of the future European central bank.
But any attempt by the Socialist party to shout too loudly about what France wanted out of EMU might frighten the German public, already nervous about giving up the mark for the euro.
The centre-right, and Chirac, has been careful to remain relatively low-key about its European demands since the start of the year, hoping they can win more from discreet negotiations.

On balance though, most economists believe a Socialist-led government would compromise on Europe issues with France's other partners in the European Union, just as the centre-right did, to make a single currency possible.
"It was a Socialist administration that started Maastricht and a Conservative administration that continued it," Godement said.
Many economists also believe the Socialists would stick to sound financial management, rather than let the deficit run out of control.
Socialist leader Lionel Jospin has pledged not to impose further austerity just to reduce the public deficit to precisely 3.0 percent of gross domestic product.
But he said on Sunday that while France needed bold economic policies, it must also be "careful about public spending".
The fact the Socialists have called for an audit of public finances if they win has suggested to some they are looking for an excuse for any spending cuts which might be needed.
Jospin has also said that even if he had to share power with the Communists, who want a new referendum on a single currency, the Socialist line on Europe would prevail.
And in the end Chirac will continue to control foreign policy -- and represent France at European summits -- even if he has to share power with a Socialist government.
